query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), the unusually high hardness and strength are governed by a predominance of edge dislocation–mediated plasticity. The inherent lattice distortions from multi‐principal element interactions increase local misfit, promoting the nucleation and thermal super‐jogging of edge dislocations that act as stronger barriers to plastic flow than conventional screw dislocations.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase refractory BCC high‐entropy alloy with balanced, multi‐principal elements (e.g., NbTaTiV or CrMoNbV systems) that exhibits significant lattice distortions from compositional complexity.
generation.intervention: Precisely vary the alloy composition and apply controlled heat treatments to adjust the lattice misfit and related distortions; conduct deformation tests (e.g., nanoindentation, tensile tests) and in situ characterization (e.g., TEM, neutron diffraction) to monitor dislocation types and density.
generation.conditions: Tests should be performed at room temperature and elevated temperatures (e.g., 673–1073 K) on alloys with comparable microstructures but differing degrees of lattice distortion. A conventional BCC alloy or a HEA engineered to minimize lattice misfit can serve as the baseline for comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions induced by the multi‐principal element arrangement, which control the type and mobility of dislocations by favoring the formation and thermal activation (super‐jogging) of edge dislocations.
generation.mechanism: The multi‐element interactions create heterogeneous strain fields that destabilize the typical screw dislocation core and facilitate edge dislocation nucleation and thermal activation. These edge dislocations, having higher lattice friction due to thermal super‐jogging barriers, impede plastic flow more effectively, leading to increased hardness and strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with enhanced lattice distortions will exhibit a higher fraction of mobile edge dislocations, a thermal strength plateau at elevated temperatures, and measurable increases (e.g., higher nanoindentation hardness and yield strength) compared to baseline alloys with lower lattice misfit and predominantly screw dislocation behavior.
generation.baseline: Conventional BCC alloys or HEAs with similar phase compositions but lower levels of compositional lattice distortion, which are expected to display traditional screw dislocation–dominated plasticity and lower hardness/strength.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for refractory HEAs with a BCC structure and significant compositional complexity. It may not apply to FCC HEAs or dual-phase alloys where other strengthening mechanisms (e.g., twin formation or interphase boundary strengthening) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of edge versus screw dislocations to overall strength and the exact temperature range over which thermal super‐jogging becomes dominant remain to be precisely calibrated. Subtle compositional variations and processing histories might also affect the mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEAs: one set engineered for higher lattice misfit (which should favor edge dislocations) and a control set with minimized lattice distortions. Subject both sets to identical heat treatments and deformation tests while performing in situ TEM and neutron diffraction to quantify the dislocation character. Correlate these findings with mechanical properties measured by nanoindentation and tensile tests at both room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: Fraction and density of edge versus screw dislocations via TEM and neutron diffraction
Hardness and yield strength (e.g., through nanoindentation and tensile testing)
Temperature-dependent strength profiles to detect a thermal strength plateau
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys designed to have enhanced lattice distortions do not show a significantly higher proportion of edge dislocations or if their mechanical properties (i.e., hardness/strength and temperature-dependence) are not measurably superior to those of the control set, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations. We use the insight and theory to perform a computationally-guided search over 107 BCC HEAs and identify over 106 possible ultra-strong high-T alloy compositions for future exploration.Subject terms: Mechanical engineering, Mechanical properties, Computational methods The strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is associated with the type of mobile dislocations.
